slides.say: Two circles with centers A and B touch each other from the outside. Their radii are eight centimeters and two centimeters. A line touches the two circles at D and C, as in the figure. What is the length of D C, in centimeters?
at: Two circles with centers A and B

slides.say: We need a length, D C, but the figure has only two circles and a line. Let's use the math way. We'll go to the givens and see what each one gives us. We'll build a right triangle, and at the end there's a short formula too.

[short pause] Let's look at the bottom part of the figure, bigger. D and C are points of tangency. Let's draw each radius to its touching point, A D and B C. That gives two right angles, because a radius is perpendicular to the tangent at its touching point.
at: Let's look at the bottom part

slides.say: A D is a radius of the big circle, eight. B C is a radius of the small circle, two. Both are perpendicular to the same line, so they're parallel to each other.

The circles touch, so let's also join the centers. A B passes through the point where the circles touch. The first part is a radius of the big circle, eight, and the second part is a radius of the small one, two. So A B is eight plus two, ten.
at: So A B is eight plus two

slides.say: Now look at A B C D. It has two right angles, at D and at C, and two parallel sides, A D and B C. It's a right trapezoid. D C is perpendicular to both parallel sides, so it's the distance between them. That's the length we want.
at: Now look at A B C D

slides.say: To use Pythagoras, we need a right triangle with D C in it, or a copy of D C. So from B, draw a line parallel to D C, until it meets A D. Call that point E.
E B C D is a rectangle, because all its angles are right angles. So E D is equal to B C, which is two. And E B is equal to D C, the length we want.
at: E B C D is a rectangle
So E D is equal to B C

slides.say: Now A E is the whole radius A D, minus E D. Eight minus two is six.
Look at the right triangle A B E. The hypotenuse A B is ten, and one leg, A E, is six. Six and ten, that's the six, eight, ten triangle, so the other leg, B E, is eight.

Let's check it with Pythagoras. The missing leg squared is the hypotenuse squared minus the other leg squared. Ten squared is a hundred. Six squared is thirty-six. A hundred minus thirty-six is sixty-four. A length is positive, so we take the positive root, eight.
B E is equal to D C, so D C is eight. Choice number two is our answer.
at: Choice number two is our answer

slides.say: [pause] Now the traps. Ten, choice number one, is A B, the distance between the centers. It's not the tangent. And six, choice number three, is only A E, the difference between the radii.
Two root thirty-four, choice number four, comes from adding the squares. Thirty-six plus a hundred is a hundred thirty-six, and the root of a hundred thirty-six is two root thirty-four.
But A B is the hypotenuse, the longest side. Two root thirty-four is more than ten, because root thirty-four is more than five. And a leg can't be longer than the hypotenuse.
at: Two root thirty-four is more than ten

slides.say: [short pause] There's also a short formula. Let's see why it works, with letters. Call the big radius capital R, and the small radius small r. The circles touch from the outside, so A B, the hypotenuse, is R plus r. And A E is R minus r.
at: the hypotenuse, is R plus r
the hypotenuse, is R plus r
And A E is R minus r
And A E is R minus r

slides.say: By Pythagoras, D C squared is the hypotenuse squared minus the leg squared. That's R plus r, squared, minus, R minus r, squared.
We know both of these from expressions. R plus r, squared, is R squared plus two R r plus r squared. R minus r, squared, is R squared minus two R r plus r squared.
Now subtract. The R squared and the r squared cancel. Taking away minus two R r adds it, so we're left with two R r plus two R r, four R r.

So D C squared is four R r. A length is positive, so D C is the root of four R r. That's two times the root of R times r. Here it's two times the root of eight times two, two times the root of sixteen. Two times four is eight, the same answer.
at: so D C is the root of four
Here it's two times the root

slides.say: Let's check it on other circles, with radii nine and four, touching from the outside. The centers are nine plus four, thirteen apart. And the difference of the radii is nine minus four, five.
Five, twelve, thirteen, so the tangent segment is twelve. And the formula gives two times the root of nine times four. That's two times the root of thirty-six, two times six, twelve. The same.
at: so the tangent segment is twelve
so the tangent segment is twelve

slides.say: So remember when it works. Two circles touch each other from the outside, and D C is the piece of a common tangent line between its two touching points. Then D C is two times the root of R times r.

slides: If the circles don't touch, but there's still a common tangent like this, cut off the same right triangle. Its hypotenuse is the distance between the centers. And if one circle is inside the other, there's no such tangent at all. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
